newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's ruler favours multinational force.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's ruler favours multinational force.

text.p: Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko on Wednesday backed the use of a multinational force to help 1.2 million refugees in Zaire but rebels said they wanted an African force.
Efforts to send aid to the refugees stranded in the east Zairean war zone were deadlocked, with Zaire telling aid agencies to keep out and the United Nations warning that many lives were threatened.
After a meeting at Mobutu's French Riviera villa, U.N. envoy Raymond Chretien quoted him as saying he would do his utmost to maintain calm in Zaire to let a multinational force work.

"President Mobutu told me Zaire would do everything possible to maintain this period of calm so that the multinational force discussed in Nairobi may be able to rapidly allow for food to reach refugees and help them return to their home countries, including of course Rwanda," Chretien said.
"He was very clear, very categorical," Chretien said.
An eight-nation African summit in Nairobi on Tuesday called for the United Nations to send a "neutral" protection force to create havens from which refugees could go home along safe corridors.

Chretien said the period of calm mentioned by Mobutu referred to a ceasefire declared by Rwanda-backed Tutsi rebels fighting Zairean troops. It was the first sign of Zairean official support for the three-week rebel truce offer.
Mobutu is convalescing in France after surgery that has kept him away for months but is expected to return home in days.

In the east of Zaire, the rebels are mainly native Tutsis who rose up two weeks ago when faced with expulsion. They are allied to others opposed to Mobutu, whose grip on power spans three decades rife with corruption.
France, pushing hardest for intervention, wants a 5,000 strong mulitnational force, its ally Spain said. Both have pledged around 1,000 troops, but Rwanda considers Paris pro-Hutu.

"I don't know why the French have to intervene here again for humanitarian purposes because we have declared a ceasefire," Laurent Kabila, self-professed leader of the rebel the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
"We are proposing not French or other forces from outside but (troops) from within the region here," Kabila told a news conference in the rebel-held eastern Zairean city of Bukavu.

French forces based in eastern Zaire intervened in western Rwanda in 1994 to set up safe havens for refugees, most of them Hutus who were fleeing civil war and reprisals for the Hutu genocide of up to one million Tutsis and Hutu moderates.

Kabila said many former Rwandan Hutu troops and militiamen and Zairean soldiers were with the refugees and wanted to use them as "cannon fodder" but the rebels wanted them regrouped for humanitarian reasons.
"But we don't want responsibility for the camps because we know that the former soldiers will infiltrate," added Kabila, a former comrade-in-arms of 1960s Marxist guerrilla Che Guevara.
In Kinshasa, Zairean spokesman Boguo Makeli said before Mobutu's talks with Chretien that Zaire was asking agencies to stop distributing any aid to refugees on Zairean soil.
"They must instead distribute aid in Rwanda and Burundi," said the spokesman, whose government wants the refugees out.
Aid dried up last week when aid workers fled fighting. The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR says many lives will be lost unless they take food and medicine back into Zaire fast.
"You can't repatriate dead refugees. We need to get in there," its spokesman Peter Kessler told Reuters in Nairobi.
But the United States, Africans and others that France and Spain want to entice in seemed lukewarm about armed intervention.

Ethiopia pledged troops for a neutral force if it was approved by the Security Council but African nations plan their next formal discussion of the force only next Monday. Britain said it was far too early to consider and analysts said post-election Washington had other things to occupy it.

Meanwhile the plight of the refugees, most of them Rwandans, worsens. Some have been without food for nearly three weeks and even the ceasefire by the rebels in Zaire has failed to ease access to those behind Zairean lines.

In the rebel-held eastern Zairean town of Goma, Zairean aid workers were unable to reach the world's largest refugee camp Mugunga because rebels said it was held by Interahamwe Hutu militiamen, who had a major role in Rwanda's 1994 genocide.
So far only 2,000 refugees have gone home to Rwanda, while 11,000 Burundian refugees were forced home by Zairean rebels.
